examTakeaway: After an ulcer is controlled, aspirin taken for coronary disease is restarted, not stopped for the long term.
scenario: A 68-year-old man had a bleeding duodenal ulcer clipped yesterday. The bleeding has stopped and his hemoglobin is stable at 9.4 g/dL. He had a myocardial infarction three years ago and has taken aspirin 81 mg daily since then. His blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. A colleague cancels the aspirin for the next six months so the ulcer can heal.
question: What should happen to the aspirin he takes for his coronary disease?
options: Restart it once hemostasis is secure, rather than withholding it for months
Stop it for six months so the mucosa can heal
Replace it with a second antiplatelet drug and never resume it
Continue it only if a new troponin is elevated
Double the dose for one week, then stop
correctAnswer: Restart it once hemostasis is secure, rather than withholding it for months
explanation:
After an ulcer is controlled, aspirin taken for coronary disease is restarted, not stopped for the long term. He already has hemostasis, a stable hemoglobin, and a secondary-prevention reason for the drug. Stopping it for six months trades a controlled ulcer for a coronary risk the 2021 guideline tells clinicians not to accept. American College of Gastroenterology Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding, 2021.

Restart it once hemostasis is secure, rather than withholding it for months
Stop it for six months so the mucosa can heal — A long hold removes the coronary protection after the bleeding is already controlled.
Replace it with a second antiplatelet drug and never resume it — The coronary indication is the existing aspirin. A substitute antiplatelet drug is not the instruction.
Continue it only if a new troponin is elevated — He does not need a new infarct to justify a drug he already takes for an old one.
Double the dose for one week, then stop — The dose stays at the prevention dose. Raising it does not treat the ulcer.
citation: American College of Gastroenterology Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding, 2021.
